## Author's thesis (paraphrased from source)

This reference covers a subset of the playbook: every page listed above was read in full, and nothing here describes pages outside it. Where a taken page links to a page outside the subset (shadow testing, load and performance testing, UI testing, synthetic monitoring, observability, the CI/CD section, the per-attribute non-functional requirement pages), the link is recorded and the linked page's content is not described. The pages are practice guidance, much of it written in the first person plural; their claims are the playbook's recommendations and assertions. Where they lean on evidence, it is a cited source (for example, the IBM cost estimate in `why-unit-tests.md`) or the authors' stated experience (for example, "In our usage" in the E2E tool comparison).

The testing pages treat tests as part of what makes code finished. The overview states: "We consider code to be incomplete if it is not accompanied by tests" [V] (docs/automated-testing/README.md, "The Fundamentals"). Its fundamentals are unit tests without external dependencies that can run before every PR merge, integration and E2E tests of the whole system run regularly, tests written early with further merging blocked when tests fail, and load or performance tests where appropriate [AP] (docs/automated-testing/README.md, "The Fundamentals"). Testing is presented as a set of techniques, each suited to an outcome, laid out in a pyramid where most tests sit at the cheap, fast base and tests grow slower and costlier to write, run and maintain toward the top [AP] (docs/automated-testing/e2e-testing/README.md, "Why E2E Testing"; docs/automated-testing/README.md, "Map of Outcomes to Testing Techniques"). Unit tests must be reliable, fast and isolated; integration, end-to-end and consumer-driven contract tests cover how components work together; smoke tests gate later stages; fault injection hardens a system against failure [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Unit Testing"; docs/automated-testing/cdc-testing/README.md, "Why Consumer-Driven Contract Testing"; docs/automated-testing/smoke-testing/README.md, "Smoke Testing"; docs/automated-testing/fault-injection-testing/README.md, "Fault Injection Testing").

The code-review pages hold that "Developers working on projects should conduct peer code reviews on every pull request (or check-in to a shared branch)." [V] (docs/code-reviews/README.md, "Code Reviews"). Code review is "a way to have a conversation about the code" [V] with three goals: improve code quality by removing defects before they reach shared branches, learn and grow, and build shared understanding of the code [AP] (docs/code-reviews/README.md, "Goals"). Automation takes the mechanical checks so that human reviewers can concentrate on business-logic correctness, test correctness, readability and maintainability, and the team's checklist of common errors [AP] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/reviewer-guidance.md, "Reviewer Guidance"). PRs should be small and focused, carry their tests, and not break the build [AP] (docs/code-reviews/pull-requests.md, "Size Guidance"; "Best Practices"). The way reviewers and authors speak to each other is treated as part of review quality [AP] (docs/code-reviews/inclusion-in-code-review.md, "Inclusion in Code Review").

The team-agreement and design pages make completion and readiness explicit. The team decides its Definition of Done together and documents it, at story, sprint and release level [AP] (docs/agile-development/team-agreements/definition-of-done.md, "Definition of Done"); the Definition of Ready is the agreement on how complete a user story must be before it is a candidate for estimation [AP] (docs/agile-development/team-agreements/definition-of-ready.md, "What it is"). Non-functional requirements should be specific, "quantitative, measurable and testable" [V], and defined early, when the cost of their impact on later design decisions is comparatively low [AP] (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "Documenting Non-Functional Requirements - Best Practices"; "Goals").

## Part I: Testing overview and test planning

### Why testing and the fundamentals

The overview gives four reasons for testing: tests find flaws; good tests document code by describing intent; automated tests save time compared with manual tests; and automated tests let a team change and refactor code safely without introducing regressions [AP] (docs/automated-testing/README.md, "Why Testing"). Its five fundamentals are stated as the team's practice: code without tests is incomplete; unit tests (defined as "tests without external dependencies") can run before every PR merge to check for regressions; integration and E2E tests exercise the whole system end to end and run regularly; "We write our tests early and block any further code merging if tests fail." [V]; and load or performance tests run where appropriate to validate behaviour under stress [AP] (docs/automated-testing/README.md, "The Fundamentals").

### Build for testing

The page says "It is important to build your application with testing in mind." [V] (docs/automated-testing/README.md, "Build for Testing"). Its eight tips [AP] (docs/automated-testing/README.md, "Build for Testing"):

- **Parameterize everything.** Make values configurable parameters with reasonable defaults rather than hard-coding them, so behaviour can be changed during testing, especially in performance testing; where a range of defaults must change together, use parameters that set "modes".
- **Document at startup.** Log all parameters when the application starts, so whoever reviews the logs knows how it is configured.
- **Log to console.** Logging to an external system such as Azure Monitor is a dependency that can fail, so console logs must be readable directly on the local system.
- **Log to external system.** In addition to console logs, log to an external system for traceability across services and durability of logs.
- **Log all activity.** Log activity such as database reads and external calls, ideally with a start message and a completion message, using log levels to manage noise.
- **Correlate distributed activities.** Pass a Correlation ID from system to system so the whole flow can be followed (the page links to an observability page outside this subset).
- **Log metadata.** Include context such as a Tenant ID, Customer ID or Order ID so logs can be filtered.
- **Log performance metrics.** Record how long functions took, even when App Insights captures dependency-call timings, so performance can be compared across compute platforms with different CPU, memory and network limits.

### Map of outcomes to testing techniques

A table maps outcomes, "the results that you may want to achieve in your validation efforts", to techniques, organised by the context the reader is working in (Development, Staging, Operation, Optimizing) [AP] (docs/automated-testing/README.md, "Map of Outcomes to Testing Techniques"). Its rows, grouped here by technique family [AP] (docs/automated-testing/README.md, "Map of Outcomes to Testing Techniques"):

- *Logical correctness and regressions* (Development): ensuring program logic is correct for expected, mainline, edge and unexpected inputs points to unit testing, functional tests, consumer-driven contract testing and integration testing; preventing regressions in logical correctness ("earlier is better") adds Rings, with the note that "each of these are expanding scopes of coverage". Documenting or enforcing valid API usage points to unit, functional and CDC tests. Proving implementation correctness ahead of or without a dependency points to unit testing with mocks or emulators, and CDC.
- *Interactions between components*: validating consumer-provider compatibility against a shared contract points to CDC; validating several components across interfaces in a call chain, including network hops, points to integration testing, end-to-end and segmented end-to-end tests.
- *Composite scenarios and user experience*: regressions in composite workflows (the example is an e-commerce "shop-and-buy" sequence of APIs) point to end-to-end and scenario tests; regression in user experience to UI automation and end-to-end testing; accessibility to the accessibility page; operability of the interface to automated UI testing with human usability observation.
- *Telemetry*: ensuring telemetry is detailed enough to trace malfunction in end-to-end flows points to distributed debug challenges and orphaned call chain analysis; checking that dashboards are correct and telemetry complete points to trace validation, stress load testing, scenario and end-to-end tests.
- *Security*: finding authentication or authorization vulnerabilities, and proving correct RBAC and claims interpretation, point to security scenarios.
- *Manual checks*: quickly validating one point of functionality manually points to manual smoke testing with tools such as postman, powershell and curl.
- *Compatibility*: proving backward compatibility with existing callers points to shadow testing (outside this subset).
- *Load, performance and capacity*: noisy-neighbour detection, seasonality, provisioned-capacity goals, user-facing performance characteristics, melt points per component and for the whole system, capacity limits, scalability curves, cost per unit load, behaviour under rapid traffic change and long-haul behaviour point to load testing (stress), spike, soak, squeeze and performance testing, with scenario tests (network partitioning) for resiliency to network errors; the load and performance testing pages are outside this subset. Finding cost savings points to squeeze tests.
- *Availability and runtime regressions*: availability drops point to synthetic transaction testing and outside-in probes; runtime-performance regressions to rings, synthetic transactions and rollback watchdogs; whether alerts notify or act correctly to synthetic transaction testing (negative cases) and load testing.
- *Comparison*: comparing a metric between two candidate implementations points to flighting and A/B testing.
- *Recovery and operations*: disaster recoverability (data corruption; loss of a data centre, "the meteor scenario", with MTTR measured) points to DR drills; failover runbooks and the impact of failover or scaling point to failover and scale drills.
- *Resilience*: discovering where a system is not resilient to "unpredictable yet inevitable failures" points to Chaos; the row's list of such failures runs from network outages and hardware failure to entries such as "renegade backhoe operators" [V].
- *Platform-specific*: unit testing Power Platform custom connectors points to the custom connector page (Part II).

The overview closes with two technology-specific links, the DevTest pattern for building containers with AzDO and Azurite for blob storage tests in a pipeline; both linked pages are outside this subset [AP] (docs/automated-testing/README.md, "Technology Specific Testing").

### Building test cases for a user story

"We should be intentional when we think about how to test our applications." [V] (docs/automated-testing/test-planning.md, "Test planning"). The page proposes building test plans for scenarios and working out test cases at the design stage of a user story, using a web site with a login portal as its running example [AP] (docs/automated-testing/test-planning.md, "Test planning"). Test cases are defined as the code for a story is designed, to ensure all acceptance criteria are met; the exercise can include developers and other stakeholders, and some cases may start manual while others are planned for automation [AP] (docs/automated-testing/test-planning.md, "Building test cases for a user story"). The page holds that the exercise does more than produce test cases: "it also helps clarify the acceptance criteria and informs how we should build the solution" [V] (docs/automated-testing/test-planning.md, "Building test cases for a user story").

Its five steps [AP] (docs/automated-testing/test-planning.md, "Building test cases for a user story"):

1. Understand the acceptance criteria, and clarify ambiguities with the product owner or stakeholders.
2. Identify test scenarios: positive and negative (happy paths and error cases) to cover edge cases, and decide what is in scope, for instance whether non-functional requirements such as security, accessibility and reliability are tested.
3. Define test cases, each documented with a title, preconditions, test steps and expected result; the test can be written in Given-When-Then form: "Given the initial context or state, When the action or event, Then the precise outcome" [V].
4. Automate where possible, focusing on hot paths and critical areas.
5. Review the test cases with peers or stakeholders and refine them on feedback.

The page gives five example test cases in Given-When-Then form [AE] (docs/automated-testing/test-planning.md, "Examples of Test Cases using the Given-When-Then Format"): login with valid credentials (positive); login with invalid credentials showing an error (negative); a login page protected against SQL injection (non-functional, security); a registration form giving clear error messages for invalid input (non-functional, usability); and a system that maintains 99.9% uptime over a month (non-functional, reliability).

### Grouping test cases into test plans

Test cases can be organised under test plans such as full regression, smoke and functional plans [AP] (docs/automated-testing/test-planning.md, "Grouping Test Cases into Test Plans"). The benefits the page lists: all aspects of the application get tested, including functional, non-functional and edge cases; clear objectives and scope; systematic management and execution; focus on the most critical areas by prioritising test cases on risk; compliance with standards and regulation in some industries; and a view of which tests matter most to automate [AP] (docs/automated-testing/test-planning.md, "Grouping Test Cases into Test Plans").

Common plans, each with a purpose and the cases it includes [AP] (docs/automated-testing/test-planning.md, "Common Test Plans"):

- *Full regression*: verify that recent changes have not adversely affected existing functionality; includes all functional, integration and system test cases and all previously reported bugs that have been fixed.
- *Smoke*: a quick check that the most critical functionality works; basic and high-priority core-feature cases.
- *Functional*: verify that each function conforms to the specification; cases for specific functionality, user interactions and business logic.
- *Area regression*: verify that changes in one area have not affected other parts; cases for the changed area and its integration points (the example is a change to the user profile model).

Further plans with their purposes [AP] (docs/automated-testing/test-planning.md, "Other Test Plan Examples"): integration (modules or services working together; data flow between components), user acceptance (business requirements met and readiness for production; real-world scenarios and end-to-end business processes), load (performance under heavy load), security (common issues such as SQL injection, XSS and CSRF; authentication and authorization), compatibility (devices, browsers and operating systems), recovery (recovery from crashes, hardware failures or other catastrophic problems; data integrity afterwards) and localization (translations and region-specific content).

To group cases into a plan: identify each plan's scope from the testing objectives, select the relevant cases, organise them into the plans, review and validate the grouping (with stakeholders if needed), and document each plan's purpose, scope and cases [AP] (docs/automated-testing/test-planning.md, "How to Group Test Cases into a Test Plan"). The page's resources are Ministry of Testing's "The One Page Test Plan" and a video on the same idea [BT] (docs/automated-testing/test-planning.md, "Resources").

## Part II: Unit testing

### What a unit test is

The page calls unit testing "a fundamental tool in every developer's toolbox" [V]: it tests code, encourages good design, reduces the chance of bugs reaching production, can serve as examples or documentation, and when properly written can improve developer efficiency [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Unit Testing"). It also says "Unit testing also is one of the most commonly misunderstood forms of testing." [V] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Unit Testing"). A unit test should be [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Unit Testing"):

- **Provably reliable**: it "should be 100% reliable so failures indicate a bug in the code" [V].
- **Fast**: it "should run in milliseconds, a whole unit testing suite shouldn't take longer than a couple seconds" [V].
- **Isolated**: "removing all external dependencies ensures reliability and speed" [V].

### Why unit tests

The README and the dedicated page both open by saying that unit tests are hard to write, harder to write well, and add development time to every feature [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Why Unit Testing"; docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/why-unit-tests.md, "Why Unit Tests"). The four reasons given [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Why Unit Testing"):

- **Reduce costs.** The later a bug is found the more expensive it is to fix, especially in production; the page cites a 2008 IBM research study that "estimates that a bug caught in production could cost 6 times as much as if it was caught during implementation" [BT] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/why-unit-tests.md, "Reduce Costs").
- **Increase developer confidence.** Many changes are small; a strong unit suite raises confidence that a change will not cause downstream bugs, and makes mechanical refactors "provably safe" when done with refactoring tools and covered by tests [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/why-unit-tests.md, "Increase Developer Confidence").
- **Speed up development.** Although tests take time to write, the suite grows into an essential part of the developer's workflow. If a developer's only testing is a long-running system test, integration tests that need a deployment, or manual testing, writing a feature takes longer; those belong in the "Outer loop", run at the PR stage or later. The Developer Inner Loop is the code, build, run, repeat cycle; unit tests inserted there give early feedback, and because they execute quickly they should not be a barrier to the loop. Tools such as Visual Studio Live Unit Testing shorten it further [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/why-unit-tests.md, "Speed Up Development").
- **Documentation as code.** Unit tests show how units are meant to be used, and "In some ways, unit tests are better than any documentation or samples because they are (or at least should be) executed with every build so there is confidence that they are not out of date." [V] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/why-unit-tests.md, "Documentation as Code").

### Design blocks and getting started

Unit testing is the lowest level of testing, with few components and dependencies [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Unit Testing Design Blocks"). Its blocks are the **system under test** (SUT), generally a method or function, kept as small as possible; **unit testing frameworks** and runners, whose base function is to organise tests and run them quickly; and **unit test code**, which "is generally short and simple, preferring repetition to adding layers and complexity to the code" [V] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Unit Testing Design Blocks"). Writing a first unit test is easier than for other test types because it needs next to no setup; frameworks differ, but the techniques and practices are described as universal [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Applying the Unit Testing"). The page notes that some techniques are more specific to strongly typed, object-oriented languages, and that functional and scripting languages have similar techniques that may look different [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Techniques").

### Techniques: abstraction, dependency injection, test-driven development

**Abstraction** generalises an exact implementation detail into a concept; for unit tests it is used to break a hard dependency and replace it with an abstraction, which then allows a mock or simulator in its place [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Abstraction"). A side effect is an abstraction with no test coverage: "you can not expect to unit test everything" [V], dependencies will always be uncovered, and so integration or functional testing should still be used, since otherwise "a change in the way the dependency functions would never be caught" [V] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Abstraction"). Wrappers around third-party dependencies should hold as little logic as possible, as a simple facade that calls the dependency [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Abstraction").

**Dependency injection** extracts dependencies from code. A dependency constructed inside the system under test creates a hard dependency that is hard to test in isolation; injecting it instead gives "inverted control" of the dependency [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Dependency Injection"). The page says Inversion of Control and Dependency Injection are hard to have one without the other, with some arguing (a link to an article on martinfowler.com) that dependency injection is a more specific way of saying inversion of control [BT] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Dependency Injection"). In languages such as C#, not using dependency injection can produce code that cannot be unit tested because mocked objects cannot be injected; keeping testability in mind from the start can save a time-intensive refactor later [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Dependency Injection"). The page also names a downside: dependency injection "can easily go overboard" [V]; coupling between interfaces remains, and passing every interface implementation into every class has as many downsides as not using it. "Being intentional with what dependencies get injected to what classes, is key to developing a maintainable system." [V] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Dependency Injection"). Frameworks such as Spring (Java) and the one built into ASP.NET Core handle the boilerplate [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Dependency Injection").

**Test-driven development** is "a technique for writing your code that will lead you to a testable design from the start" [V]: list the behaviours the system should have, take one, write its test, change the system to pass it, and repeat until the list is exhausted. The page claims the approach has "the benefit of guaranteeing a testable design is built into the system since the test was written first" [V] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Test-Driven Development").

### Best practices

- **Arrange/Act/Assert.** Divide a test into three sections: Arrange (variables, mocks, interfaces and state), Act (run the system under test), Assert (check the system acted appropriately). The page says this makes tests readable and familiar to future developers, and illustrates it with a C# test `TrySomething_NoElements_ReturnsFalse` [AP] [AE] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Arrange/Act/Assert").
- **Keep tests small and test only one thing**, so a failure is easy to diagnose; with Arrange/Act/Assert, think of it as testing one thing in the Act phase. The page records "some disagreement" between "assert one thing" and "test one state, with multiple asserts if needed", says there is no right answer, and concludes: "Consistency when writing your tests one way or the other is more important!" [V] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Keep Tests Small and Test Only One Thing").
- **Use a standard naming convention.** Without one, test names are not descriptive enough or are duplicated across classes. The page's own convention is `UnitName_StateUnderTest_ExpectedResult`; others are possible, and the point is to be consistent and descriptive. A descriptive name tells the reader what was expected and which state failed, which helps in CI/CD systems where the test name may be all that is known [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Using a Standard Naming Convention for All Unit Tests").

### Things to avoid in unit tests

Three pitfalls [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Things to Avoid"):

- **Sleeps.** A sleep can indicate the code is calling a dependency it should not. If code is flaky without the sleep, find out why and remove the flakiness with a more reliable way to signal state changes. Sleeps also break the tenet that tests run in milliseconds; tests that take seconds become cumbersome to run.
- **Reading from disk.** Storing an expected value in a file creates a dependency on the system drive and breaks the tenets of isolation and 100% reliability; file access can cause intermittent failures, and the need may signal that the test or unit is too complex.
- **Calling third-party APIs.** Code you do not control cannot be known for certain, so abstract it out; such calls are "generally a sign that the design of the system is not entirely testable" [V]. Wrap third-party calls in interfaces so they are not invoked in unit tests.

### Frameworks and tools

Unit test frameworks are constantly changing; choose by which feature set fits the project (the page links Wikipedia's list of frameworks) [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Test Frameworks"). Many projects add a mock framework alongside; the page says this "should not be something that is added without considering the broader implications and risks associated with heavy usage of mocks" [V] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Mock Frameworks"). Tools for continuous test running with in-line coverage, said to make the inner loop extremely fast and TDD easy: Visual Studio Live Unit Testing, Wallaby.js, Infinitest (Java) and PyCrunch (Python) [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Tools").

### Transferring responsibility to integration tests

In some situations integration tests may be brought into the inner development loop to provide enough coverage; the prerequisite is that they run at a speed comparable to unit tests, locally and in CI [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Transferring Responsibility to Integration Tests"). The page says modern frameworks such as .NET or Spring Boot, combined with the right mocking or stubbing of external dependencies, enable this [AP]. Integration tests usually prove only that modules connect as designed, but their coverage can be extended to verify correct behaviour, and "The responsibility of providing a sufficient branch and line code coverage can be transferred from unit tests to integration tests." [V] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Transferring Responsibility to Integration Tests"). One integration scenario then covers a whole flow that several unit tests would otherwise cover; for an API, each request's HTTP response and content are verified, covering both the integration of components and the correctness of business logic [AE]. The page lists advantages: black-box testing without knowledge of internals, refactoring with no impact on tests, and TDD applied at a higher level, giving a process driven by acceptance tests. Unit tests still matter for dictating testable design at a lower level and for complex business logic and corner cases [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Transferring Responsibility to Integration Tests"). (The integration-testing page, in Part III, advises against testing business logic in integration tests.)

### Conclusion of the unit-testing page

"Unit testing is extremely important, but it is also not the silver bullet" [V]; proper unit tests are only part of a well-tested system, but they help with design, catch regressions and bugs, and increase developer velocity [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Conclusion"). The single resource is Microsoft's "Unit Testing Best Practices" for .NET [BT] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Resources").

### Worked example: test-driven development

The TDD page writes one test at a time, then the minimal system code to pass it: "It's important to write the bare minimum of code necessary" [V] even if that code is not yet correct, refactoring once the test passes; the page says all code written is covered, so minimal changes can continue with confidence [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/tdd-example.md, "Test-Driven Development Example"). The example builds a C# `ValidatePassword` function, specified as "a string larger than 8 characters containing at least one number" [V], through Red-Green-Refactor [AE] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/tdd-example.md, "Test-Driven Development Example"):

- A null-input test fails against a stub (the "Red" step); throwing `ArgumentNullException` unconditionally makes it pass (the "Green" step), and the page accepts that the function does not yet really work.
- A short-input test (`"abc"` returns false) leads to a null check plus `return false`. The page notes that it was the second test, not the null test, that led to the `if` statement for the null check, and recommends adding the negative test before the positive one so both cases are covered.
- A positive test uses `"abcdefgh1"`. The page stresses making tests resilient to future changes: `"abcdefgh"` would pass now but fail incorrectly once the number rule is added.
- A first passing implementation returns true when the length exceeds 8; the first "Refactor" step inverts the condition to return false when the length is under 8, which the page presents as a provably safe refactor that does not change what the function returns, usually done with IDE tooling.
- A negative test for a valid-length string without a digit (`"abcdefghij"`) leads to a LINQ `Any(char.IsDigit)` check, then a refactor combining the two conditions.

The page ends by saying the function has 100% test coverage of positive and negative scenarios, that a switch to a regex implementation would leave all tests passing and valid, and that a design written test-first is "guaranteed" to be testable [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/tdd-example.md, "Test-Driven Development Example").

### Test doubles: stubs, mocks and fakes

The mocking page treats replacing a system's dependencies with an implementation you control as a key part of unit testing. A test double is a generic term for any "pretend" object used in place of a real one [AP], and the page adopts Martin Fowler's definitions of the terms [BT] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Mocking in Unit Tests"). Mocks are the most commonly used double, but "there are many cases where Mocks perhaps are not the best choice and Fakes should be considered instead" [V] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Mocking in Unit Tests").

**Stubs** give predetermined behaviour in place of real behaviour, implementing the dependency's abstract class or interface with the logic the client expects; they suit cases where all clients expect the same responses, such as a third-party service [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Stubs"). "The key concept here is that stubs should never fail a unit or integration test where a mock can." [V] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Stubs"). They need no framework, though mocking frameworks often build them, and are commonly combined with dependency injection; a Python example overrides a service with a stub through a DI container [AE]. Because nearly every test needs its own stubs, they become repetitive boilerplate, and codebases rarely use stubs alone. Upside: no framework, easy to set up; downside: much rewritten boilerplate [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Stubs").

**Mocks**, in Fowler's description, are pre-programmed objects with expectations that form a specification of the calls they expect, such as how many times a sub-method is called or how arguments are passed [BT] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Mocks"). Mocking frameworks are abundant for every language and, the page says, make tests easy to write while still encouraging good unit testing practices [AP]. The page's distinction is that "mocks do behavioral verification, whereas other test doubles do state verification" [V]: behavioural verification tests that the implementation is as expected, while state verification checks only inputs and outputs (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Mocks"). "The major downside to behavioral verification is that it is tied to the implementation." [V] If tests must be updated whenever the implementation changes, the confidence that passing tests signal a safe change is lost, bugs can enter the test code, and development time and frustration rise [AP]. Its example: a method making 5 web service calls is tested by checking those 5 calls; when the API changes to need one call, the test fails and must be rewritten, lowering confidence in the change [AE] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Mocks"). The page grants that "Some would argue" such a test was poor anyway, but holds that mocking frameworks allowing these verifications encourage such tests to be written: "By not using a mock framework that allows this, you never run the risk of writing tests that are validating the implementation." [V] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Mocks"). Upsides: easy to write, encourages testable design; downsides: maintainability problems from behavioural testing, and usually a framework (or much boilerplate) [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Upsides to Mocking"; "Downsides to Mocking").

**Fakes** have working implementations that take some shortcut unsuitable for production; the common example is an in-memory database, which keeps unit tests fast without breaking abstraction [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Fakes"). Fakes take longer to write and can carry their own unit tests, which the page says increases confidence further because the double itself has been tested. Like mocks they promote testable design, but need no framework. Fakes often get "promoted" to product code, or start there; a library or API that ships a fake spares its users from writing their own mocks. Upsides: no framework, testable design, effort not wasted; downside: more time to implement [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Fakes"; "Upsides to Fakes"; "Downsides to Fakes").

### Mocking best practices

- **Dependency injection.** Without testability in mind from the start, writing tests may require a time-intensive refactor; in languages such as C#, not using dependency injection is a common cause of non-testable code, so use it so mocks can be injected into the SUT [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Dependency Injection").
- **Assertions.** Assert the right things, not necessarily many things. When a method passes a mocked result straight back, asserting on the return value mainly checks that the mock was set up correctly [AP]. The page's `SearchController.GetName` example shows a test that would still pass if the method simply returned the literal value, and would fail if the mock were set up wrong though the logic were sound [AE]. The rule: "make assertions on your logic, not mock return values" [V]; here, use `Verify` to check that the search client was called with the right parameters (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Assertions"). Glue code with as little logic as the example "don't always have to be unit tested and might instead be covered by integration tests" [V]; where there is more logic, verify mock calls and assert on the parts of the mock result the SUT modified [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Assertions").
- **Callbacks.** Setting up mocks to match complex parameters is time-consuming and error-prone: missing one attribute means the mock is not called. Specify only the parameters that distinguish calls, use an `any` matcher for the rest, capture the actual argument in a callback, and assert only on the attributes the SUT influences (the example asserts on `SearchMode` and `QueryType`). The page says this is more explicit about what the test cares about and more efficient to set up [AP] [AE] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Callbacks").

The page's conclusion: test doubles are "an essential part of having a healthy test suite" [V]; weigh the future implications of a mocking framework from the start, since "Sometimes certain features of mocking frameworks seem essential, but usually that is a sign that the code itself is not abstracted enough if it requires a framework." [V] Its recommendation: "If possible, starting without a mocking framework and attempting to create fake implementations will lead to a more healthy code base" [V]; where that is not possible, the onus is on the team's technical leaders to find mocks that are overused, rely too much on implementation details, or do not test the right things [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Conclusion").

### Worked example: writing a unit test

The authoring page takes a C# `Configuration` class that reads startup options from a `.config` file and has three problems: a bug with no unit tests to catch it because the class reads a file, no way to unit test code that depends on it, and a future need to load configuration from the cloud over a REST API. The bug: multiple empty lines in the file throw `IndexOutOfRangeException` [AE] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/authoring-example.md, "Writing a Unit Test").

- **Abstraction.** Rather than abstract the file system wholesale, the page asks why the file is needed and abstracts "the *concept* rather than the implementation" [AP]: a configuration reader returning lines, expressed as an `IConfigurationReader` interface with a `FileConfigurationReader` implementation. The dependency on the file system remains at this point, abstracted out but not yet broken [AE] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/authoring-example.md, "Abstraction").
- **Dependency injection.** Constructor injection passes an `IConfigurationReader` into `Configuration`, so whatever creates the object controls which reader it receives: an example of "inversion of control". Injecting the interface rather than the concrete class is what breaks the hard-coded dependency on `File` [AE] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/authoring-example.md, "Dependency Injection").
- **First tests.** Instead of a mock, the page writes a concrete `PassThroughConfigurationReader` that returns the string array it was given, pointing to the mocking page for why that may be better than mocking. The first tests describe current behaviour (an empty config throws `KeyNotFoundException`; a correct line sets the property) [AE] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/authoring-example.md, "Writing our first unit tests").
- **Fixing the bug.** The page notes that the tests pass with 100% coverage yet the bug shows not all inputs are covered, and that `KeyNotFoundException` is an implementation detail. New tests state the intended behaviour (empty config and malformed lines throw `InvalidOperationException`; a value may contain further equals signs; blank lines are ignored), leaving 4 failing and 1 passing; the fixed `Initialize` filters blank lines, splits on the first `=` only, and throws on empty or malformed input [AE] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/authoring-example.md, "Fixing the Bug").
- **Untestable code.** `FileConfigurationReader` has 0% coverage, which the page calls expected: it is kept as light as possible, with no logic beyond calling the third-party dependency, as an instance of the facade pattern [AE] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/authoring-example.md, "Untestable Code").
- **Testable design.** The future web-API source now needs only a `WebApiConfigurationReader`. "That is one of the benefits of testable design" [V]: dependencies that might change are already abstracted. The page adds that the three readers could be cascaded (web API when online, local file otherwise, the pass-through reader as a hard-coded default) [AE] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/authoring-example.md, "Testable Design and Future Improvements").

### Custom connector testing

For Power Platform custom connectors, the page names two unit-level verifications: validating the OpenAPI schema that defines the connector, and validating that the schema carries everything the certified-connector process needs (optional, but necessary to publish a certified connector) [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/custom-connector.md, "Unit Testing"). It suggests swagger-cli among schema validators listed at openapi.tools, and paconn-cli, whose validate command shows information missing from the connector definition [AP] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/custom-connector.md, "Unit Testing").

## Part III: Testing components together: integration, end-to-end and contract tests

### Integration testing

Integration testing determines how well individually developed components or modules communicate, confirming that an aggregate works together correctly or exposing erroneous behaviour between units [AP] (docs/automated-testing/integration-testing/README.md, "Integration Testing"). Because components may be developed in isolation, and complex systems combine databases, APIs, interfaces and external systems, integration tests expose system-level issues "such as broken database schemas or faulty third-party API integration" [V]; the page says they ensure higher coverage and serve as an important feedback loop [AP] (docs/automated-testing/integration-testing/README.md, "Why Integration Testing").

The page's example is a banking application with login, transfers and current-balance modules developed independently: one test checks that a logged-in mock user lands on the correct balance; another performs a transfer, checks sufficient funds and the updated balance; the login module may be mocked if it is not yet complete [AE] (docs/automated-testing/integration-testing/README.md, "Integration Testing Design Blocks"). Integration testing is done by the developer or QA tester. In the past it always came after unit and before system and E2E testing; integration tests are fewer than unit tests, usually slower, and more expensive to set up and develop. The page says that now, a team following agile principles can run them before or after unit tests, early and often, and they can use mock data to simulate a complete system [AP] (docs/automated-testing/integration-testing/README.md, "Integration Testing Design Blocks"). It distinguishes: "Integration testing confirms a group of components work together as intended from a technical perspective, while acceptance testing confirms a group of components work together as intended from a business scenario." [V] (docs/automated-testing/integration-testing/README.md, "Integration Testing Design Blocks").

Before writing integration tests, engineers identify the components and their intended behaviours, inputs and outputs, and the architecture must be fully documented or specified somewhere easily referenced, such as an architecture diagram [AP] (docs/automated-testing/integration-testing/README.md, "Applying Integration Testing"). Two main techniques [AP] (docs/automated-testing/integration-testing/README.md, "Big Bang"; "Incremental Testing"; "Top Down"; "Bottom Up"):

- **Big Bang**: all components tested as a single unit; best for small systems, since in a large one failed tests are hard to localise, and it needs every component finished, which may delay testing (figure "Big Bang Integration Testing").
- **Incremental**: two or more logically related components tested as a unit, then more added until all are tested. *Top down* tests higher-level components following the control flow, with stubs emulating unfinished lower-level modules (figure "Top Down Integration Testing"); *bottom up* tests lower-level modules together, with drivers emulating higher-level ones (figure "Bottom Up Integration Testing"). A sandwich or hybrid model combines the two.

Things to avoid [AP] (docs/automated-testing/integration-testing/README.md, "Things to Avoid"): developers trade integration coverage against engineering cycles; with mock dependencies, test data and multiple environments, too many integration tests become infeasible to maintain and less meaningful; too much mocking slows the suite, makes scaling hard, and may signal that acceptance or E2E tests suit the scenario better. Integration tests of complex systems need high maintenance. The page instructs: "Avoid testing business logic in integration tests by keeping test suites separate." [V] Do not test beyond the task's acceptance criteria, clean up resources each test creates, and "avoid writing tests in a production environment. Instead, write them in a scaled-down copy environment." [V] (docs/automated-testing/integration-testing/README.md, "Things to Avoid").

Tools named for automating integration tests: JUnit, Robot Framework, moq, Cucumber, Selenium and Behave (Python) [AP] (docs/automated-testing/integration-testing/README.md, "Integration Testing Frameworks and Tools"). The conclusion: integration tests can cover two components, a sub-system, a whole system or a collection of systems; they should be written frequently throughout the lifecycle with an appropriate amount of mocked dependencies and test data; and because they prove independently developed modules interface as designed, they increase confidence and provide "a path for a system that deploys and scales" [V] (docs/automated-testing/integration-testing/README.md, "Conclusion"). Resources include a book, *Software Testing: Principles and Practices*, and articles on approaches, pros and cons, and mocks and stubs [BT] (docs/automated-testing/integration-testing/README.md, "Resources").

### End-to-end testing

End-to-end testing tests a functional and data application flow made of several sub-systems working together from start to end; because those systems may be built in different technologies by different teams or organisations, testing one system alone would not suffice (figure "End to End Testing") [AP] (docs/automated-testing/e2e-testing/README.md, "E2E Testing"). Sub-systems may sit inside or outside the organisation and have different release cycles, so a fault in any of them can adversely affect the whole system "leading to its collapse" [V] (docs/automated-testing/e2e-testing/README.md, "Why E2E Testing").

The page's pyramid figure ("E2E Testing Pyramid") is taken from Kent C. Dodds' blog, described as a combination of pyramids from Martin Fowler's blog and the Google Testing Blog [BT]. "The majority of your tests are at the bottom of the pyramid." [V] Moving up, the number of tests falls and tests get "slower and more expensive to write, run, and maintain" [V] (docs/automated-testing/e2e-testing/README.md, "Why E2E Testing").

Design blocks (figure "E2E Testing Design Framework") [AP] (docs/automated-testing/e2e-testing/README.md, "E2E Testing Design Blocks"; "User Functions"; "Conditions"; "Test Cases"):

- *User functions*: list user-initiated functions and their interconnected sub-systems; track each function's actions and input and output data; find relations between functions; find whether functions are independent or reusable.
- *Conditions*: prepare a set of conditions for every user function; timing, data conditions and other factors can be treated as parameters.
- *Test cases*: one or more test cases per scenario to test every functionality of the user functions, automated through the CI/CD pipeline where possible with each build tracked in AzDO; every condition enlisted as a separate test case.

E2E testing goes through formal planning, execution and closure [AP] (docs/automated-testing/e2e-testing/README.md, "Applying the E2E Testing"): *planning* (business and functional requirement analysis, test plan and test case development, a production-like environment, test data, exit criteria, and choice of testing methods); *prerequisites* (system testing complete for all participating systems, all sub-systems combined into a complete application, a production-like environment ready); *execution* (execute cases, register results and decide pass or fail, report bugs, re-verify fixes); and *closure* (test report, evaluation of exit criteria, phase closure). Four common metrics [AP] (docs/automated-testing/e2e-testing/README.md, "Test Metrics"): test case preparation status (ready versus total), frequent test progress (executed on a regular cadence, such as weekly, versus target), defects status (percentages of open and closed defects by severity and priority, tracked in a tool such as an AzDO backlog and dashboard query), and test environment availability (time used versus scheduled allocation).

Six frameworks and tools are described [AP] (docs/automated-testing/e2e-testing/README.md, "E2E Testing Frameworks and Tools"):

- **Gauge**: free and open source, with Markdown-based syntax, cross-platform and cross-language support, plugins, data-driven execution, IDE support and HTML, JSON and XML reporting.
- **Robot Framework**: generic open-source automation with human-readable keywords, extensible in Python or Java. The page compares it with Gauge from the authors' experience: "In our usage, we found the VS Code Intellisense offered with Gauge to be much more stable than the offerings for Robot." [V] They also found Robot's syntax less readable than Gauge's, which reads more like an English sentence, and note that Gauge's markup files can generate a function stub for a test definition, which Robot cannot [AE] (docs/automated-testing/e2e-testing/README.md, "2. Robot Framework").
- **TestCraft**: described as a codeless Selenium test automation platform; the page says its AI technology and visual modelling allow faster test creation and execution while eliminating test maintenance overhead [AP].
- **Ranorex Studio**: end-to-end automation for desktop, web and mobile, codeless or with a full IDE, with external data inputs, parallel or Selenium Grid runs, and AzDO pipeline integration [AP].
- **Katalon Studio**: web, API, mobile and desktop automation built on Selenium and Appium, integrable into CI/CD. The page states that Katalon "is endorsed by Gartner, IT professionals, and a large testing community" [V] and notes that, at the time of writing, its AzDO extension was not available for Linux [AP].
- **BugBug.io**: a Chrome-extension-based tool for web applications, aimed at simplicity and non-technical maintainers; the page says it can save money on hiring a QA engineer [AP].

The conclusion says E2E verification plays an important role in any commercial release because it tests the whole application in an environment that imitates real-world use (network communication, middleware and back-end interaction), and that "the E2E test is often performed manually as the cost of automating such test cases is too high to be afforded by any organization" [V]; the goal is to streamline E2E testing with full and semi-automation, which is where the listed tools come in [AP] (docs/automated-testing/e2e-testing/README.md, "Conclusion").

### End-to-end testing methods

- **Horizontal test**: runs across the context of multiple applications, and is described as used very commonly. In the example of a data ingest management system (figure "Horizontal Test"), inbound data from various sources flows into a horizontal Extract-Transform-Load pipeline (gateway API, transformation, validation, storage) tracked end to end, with logging, auditing and authentication treated as optional and not important for the overall E2E test case [AP] [AE] (docs/automated-testing/e2e-testing/testing-methods.md, "Horizontal Test").
- **Vertical test**: the most critical transactions are verified from start to finish, layer by layer from top to bottom; in the example of a web application using middleware to reach back-end resources (figure "Vertical Test"), each tier is tested with the connected layers above and below. These scenarios need proper validation and dedicated automated testing, so "this method is much more difficult" [V] (docs/automated-testing/e2e-testing/testing-methods.md, "Vertical Test").

Design guidelines for E2E test cases: design from the end user's perspective, focus on existing features, consider multiple scenarios to create multiple test cases, and create different sets of cases for multiple scenarios [AP] (docs/automated-testing/e2e-testing/testing-methods.md, "E2E Test Cases Design Guidelines").

### Comparison of unit, integration, system and end-to-end testing

The comparison page tabulates "the most critical characteristics and differences" [V] between the four kinds and when to apply each [AP] (docs/automated-testing/e2e-testing/testing-comparison.md, "Unit vs Integration vs System vs E2E Testing"):

| | Unit | Integration | System | E2E |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Scope | Modules, APIs | Modules, interfaces | Application, system | All sub-systems, network dependencies, services and databases |
| Size | Tiny | Small to medium | Large | X-Large |
| Environment | Development | Integration test | QA test | Production-like |
| Data | Mock data | Test data | Test data | Copy of real production data |
| System under test | Isolated unit test | Interfaces and data flow between modules | Particular system as a whole | Application flow start to end |
| Scenarios | Developer perspectives | Developer and IT Pro tester perspectives | Developer and QA tester perspectives | End-user perspectives |
| When | After each build | After unit testing | Before E2E, after unit and integration | After system testing |
| Automated or manual | Automated | Manual or automated | Manual or automated | Manual |

### Consumer-driven contract testing

Consumer-driven contract testing (CDC) tests components in isolation "while ensuring that provider components are compatible with the expectations that consumer components have of them" [V] (docs/automated-testing/cdc-testing/README.md, "Consumer-Driven Contract Testing (CDC)"). It aims to overcome drawbacks of automated E2E tests, which the page lists, linking a Pactflow article: they are slow, break easily, are expensive and hard to maintain, and for larger systems may be hard or impossible to run outside a dedicated environment [BT] (docs/automated-testing/cdc-testing/README.md, "Why Consumer-Driven Contract Testing"). Testing best practice suggests few E2E tests relative to cheaper, faster, more stable integration and unit tests, yet the page says experience shows "many teams end up writing too many E2E tests" [V] (linking the Google Testing Blog). The page gives one reason: E2E tests give developers the highest confidence to release because they test the real system [AP] (docs/automated-testing/cdc-testing/README.md, "Why Consumer-Driven Contract Testing").

CDC tests component interactions in isolation using mocks that conform to a shared understanding documented in a "contract", agreed between consumer and provider and regularly verified against a real provider instance. The page says this partitions a large system into pieces tested individually, giving simpler, fast and stable tests that also give confidence to release [AR] (docs/automated-testing/cdc-testing/README.md, "Why Consumer-Driven Contract Testing"). "Some E2E tests are still required to verify the system as a whole when deployed in the real environment, but most functional interactions between components can be covered with CDC tests." [V] CDC began with RESTful APIs, but the page says the pattern scales to all consumer-provider systems and tooling exists for protocols besides HTTP [AP] (docs/automated-testing/cdc-testing/README.md, "Why Consumer-Driven Contract Testing").

In the consumer-driven approach (linking Ian Robinson's article on martinfowler.com), the consumer drives changes to the contract; the page concedes this "may sound counterintuitive" [V] but says it helps providers build APIs that fit consumers' real requirements rather than guessing them in advance [AP] (docs/automated-testing/cdc-testing/README.md, "Consumer-Driven Contract Testing Design Blocks"). The building blocks, in development-cycle order (figure "CDC testing") [AP] (docs/automated-testing/cdc-testing/README.md, "Consumer Tests with Provider Mock"; "Contract"; "Provider Contract Verification"):

1. **Consumer tests with provider mock.** Consumers write integration tests against a provider mock in their CI pipeline, defining expected responses; this is how the consumer defines the contract it expects.
2. **Contract.** Contracts are generated from the provider mock's expectations after a successful run; frameworks such as Pact define a JSON contract specification of request/response pairs plus metadata. "Contracts are not a replacement for a discussion between the consumer and provider team." [V] This is the moment for that discussion; the tests and contract are refined with the provider team, then versioned and stored centrally. Contracts complement API specifications such as OpenAPI: a specification describes structure and format, a contract specifies that a given request expects a given response, and the specification can help write the contract and validate it.
3. **Provider contract verification.** A separate provider pipeline verifies contracts against real provider responses and fails if they differ, for one of two causes: invalid consumer expectations, or a broken provider implementation (missing functionality or a regression). The page says CDC makes it easy to pinpoint the affected consumer or provider, which it contrasts with the debugging pain of an E2E approach.

Tools: Pact, which mocks responses in the consumer codebase and verifies interactions in the provider codebase, was originally written in Ruby, has wrappers for many languages, and "Pact is the de-facto standard to use when working with CDC." [V]; and Spring Cloud Contract, with easy Spring integration and support for non-Spring and non-JVM parties [AP] (docs/automated-testing/cdc-testing/README.md, "CDC Testing Frameworks and Tools").

The conclusion lists benefits: less maintenance, by testing interactions in isolation without a complex integrated environment, especially as interactions grow (figure "CDC VS E2E tests"); close collaboration between consumer and provider teams; and contracts as a formal record of shared understanding, so "the contract repository serves as a live documentation of all consumer-provider interactions of a system" [V]. Drawbacks: an extra testing layer needing investment in team education, and a scope that must be set carefully to avoid blurring CDC with higher-level functional testing: "Contract tests are not the place to verify internal business logic and correctness of the consumer." [V] (docs/automated-testing/cdc-testing/README.md, "Conclusion").

## Part IV: Gating and hardening: smoke and fault-injection tests

### Smoke testing

Smoke tests, also called Sanity, Acceptance or Build/Release Verification tests, are a sub-type of system or functional tests usually used as gates that verify an application's readiness as a preliminary step; an application that passes is stable enough for the next stages of testing or deployment [AP] (docs/automated-testing/smoke-testing/README.md, "Smoke Testing"). Their goal is to save time by finding out as early as possible whether an application works; if it fails, the rest of the integration or deployment chain can be abandoned. They do not aim at full coverage but at a few quick acceptance invocations the application should always answer correctly [AP] (docs/automated-testing/smoke-testing/README.md, "Problem Addressed"). They cover only the most critical path, should not be used to test the application's behaviour, keep execution time and complexity minimal, and can be formed from a subset of the integration or E2E tests [AP]. "The golden rule of a good smoke test is that it saves time on validating that the application is acceptable to a stage where better, more thorough testing will begin." [V] (docs/automated-testing/smoke-testing/README.md, "ROI Tipping Point").

The page applies smoke tests to the local dev desktop (manual check), build pipelines (a small set of integration tests before the full suite), non-production and production deployments (for example, a curl to the API asserting a 200 response before a resource-consuming load test) and PR validation (deploying the application chart to a test namespace and validating the release) [AE] (docs/automated-testing/smoke-testing/README.md, "Applicable to"). "Smoke testing is a low-effort, high-impact step to ship more reliable software." [V] The page recommends considering smoke testing among the first stages to implement when planning continuously integrated and delivered systems [AP] (docs/automated-testing/smoke-testing/README.md, "Conclusion").

### Fault injection testing

Fault injection testing deliberately introduces errors and faults into a system to validate and harden its stability and reliability. "The goal is to improve the system's design for resiliency and performance under intermittent failure conditions over time." [V] (docs/automated-testing/fault-injection-testing/README.md, "Fault Injection Testing"). Systems need to be resilient to the conditions behind inevitable production disruptions; modern applications depend on infrastructure, platform, network, third-party software and APIs, each of which may fail and propagate failure through its interactions [AP] (docs/automated-testing/fault-injection-testing/README.md, "Problem Addressed"). Fault injection increases coverage and validates robustness and error handling at build time or run time, "embracing failure" as part of the lifecycle, and helps teams design and continuously validate for known and unknown failure, redundancy, and retry and back-off [AP] (docs/automated-testing/fault-injection-testing/README.md, "Problem Addressed").

It applies at three levels [AP] [AE] (docs/automated-testing/fault-injection-testing/README.md, "Applicable to"): **software** (error-handling paths, in-process memory management; edge-case unit and integration tests and stress or soak load tests); **protocol** (vulnerabilities in interfaces such as command-line parameters or APIs; fuzzing with invalid, unexpected or random input); and **infrastructure** (outages, networking issues, hardware failure; shutting down VMs, crashing processes, expiring certificates, adding latency), where testing relies on statistical observation over time of deviations during the fault and of recovery time.

Its terminology [AP] (docs/automated-testing/fault-injection-testing/README.md, "Terminology"): a **fault** is "The adjudged or hypothesized cause of an error." [V]; an **error** is the part of system state that may cause a subsequent failure; a **failure** is an event where the delivered service deviates from correct state; and in the **fault-error-failure cycle**, which the page calls a key mechanism in dependability (linking Wikipedia), a fault may cause an error, each new error acts as a fault within the system boundary, and errors observed at the boundary are termed failures. Fault injection is described as an advanced form of testing that subjects the system to different failure modes, where the engineer may know the expected outcome in advance (as in release validation) or may be exploring for issues to mitigate [AP] (docs/automated-testing/fault-injection-testing/README.md, "Fault Injection Testing Basics"). The page distinguishes it from chaos engineering: fault injection is "a specific approach to testing one condition" [V]; chaos engineering, which it says was coined by Netflix, "is a practice for generating new information" [V]; the two overlap in concerns and tooling, and chaos engineering often uses fault injection (docs/automated-testing/fault-injection-testing/README.md, "Fault Injection and Chaos Engineering").

**In the development cycle**, the page calls fault injection an effective way to find security bugs, noting that the Microsoft Security Development Lifecycle requires fuzzing at every untrusted interface of every product, and penetration testing that introduces faults [BT]. Automated fault injection in CI promotes a Shift-Left approach. Examples: fuzzing tools in CI; existing end-to-end scenario tests (integration or stress) augmented with fault injection; regression and acceptance tests written from fixed issues or resolved incidents; ad-hoc manual fault validation for new features in the dev environment [AP] (docs/automated-testing/fault-injection-testing/README.md, "Fault injection testing in the development cycle").

**In the release cycle**, like synthetic monitoring tests (outside this subset), fault injection is part of Shift-Right testing, using safe methods in production or pre-production. Because distributed, cloud-based services are hard to simulate outside production, "Testers are encouraged to run tests where it really matters, on a live system with customer traffic." [V] Such tests rely on observability and are usually statistical; the sample steps are: measure and define a steady state, hypothesise the behaviour under a fault, introduce real-world fault events, measure and compare with the baseline, document the process and observations, and act on the result [AP] (docs/automated-testing/fault-injection-testing/README.md, "Fault Injection Testing in the Release Cycle").

**In Kubernetes**, the page says fault injection "has become inevitable" [V] as Kubernetes has advanced as an infrastructure platform; clusters run varied workloads in different languages and are managed differently from traditional infrastructure, so tools need: easy injection into pods, fast installation in the cluster, YAML-based configuration, easy customisation with custom resources, workflows to deploy workloads and faults, maintainability, and telemetry integration [AP] (docs/automated-testing/fault-injection-testing/README.md, "Fault Injection Testing in Kubernetes").

**Best practices.** Experimenting in production tests a live system with real traffic but "has the potential to cause unnecessary customer pain" [V]. A failed test will likely affect production, so "Thinking about the Blast Radius of the effect, should the test fail, is a crucial step to conduct beforehand." [V] (docs/automated-testing/fault-injection-testing/README.md, "Best Practices and Advice"). Practices to minimise risk [AP] (docs/automated-testing/fault-injection-testing/README.md, "Best Practices and Advice"): run tests in a non-production environment first, with synthetic workload; use fault injection as gates at different CD pipeline stages; deploy and test on Blue/Green and Canary deployments, using traffic shadowing ("Dark Traffic") to bring customer traffic to the staging slot; balance collecting real results against affecting as few production users as possible; use defensive design such as circuit breaking and bulkheads; agree a budget, in terms of a Service Level Objective, as an investment in chaos and fault injection; and grow the risk incrementally, hardening the core first and expanding in layers, with progress locked in by automated regression tests.

**Tools.** Fuzzing: OneFuzz (Microsoft's open-source, self-hosted fuzzing-as-a-service), AFL and WinAFL (Google Project Zero), and WebScarab (OWASP, found in Kali Linux). Chaos: Azure Chaos Studio (described as in preview), Chaos Toolkit (with an Azure actions and probes kit), Kraken (OpenShift, maintained by Red Hat), Chaos Monkey (Netflix's platform, which the page says popularised chaos engineering and does not support Azure out of the box), Simmy (a .NET chaos library integrated with Polly), Litmus (a CNCF tool for Kubernetes), and an ISE dev blog post showing Polly and Simmy in a hypothesis-driven approach [AP] (docs/automated-testing/fault-injection-testing/README.md, "Fuzzing"; "Chaos").

**Conclusion.** The page quotes the principles of chaos: "The harder it is to disrupt the steady-state, the more confidence we have in the behavior of the system." [V] [BT] It says fault injection increases resilience and confidence and is used across the industry before and during delivery, but "Fault injection is a powerful tool and should be used with caution." [V] It cites the Cloudflare 30-minute global outage, caused by deploying code meant to be "dark launched", as showing the importance of curtailing blast radius in experiments [BT] (docs/automated-testing/fault-injection-testing/README.md, "Conclusion"). Resources include posts by Mark Russinovich and Cindy Sridharan and Azure Architecture Framework pages [BT] (docs/automated-testing/fault-injection-testing/README.md, "Resources").

## Part V: Code reviews and pull requests

### Goals

Peer review should happen on every pull request or check-in to a shared branch [AP] (docs/code-reviews/README.md, "Code Reviews"). Its three goals: improve code quality "by identifying and removing defects before they can be introduced into shared code branches" [V]; learn and grow, through exposure to unfamiliar design patterns or languages and breaking bad habits; and shared understanding of the project's code [AP] (docs/code-reviews/README.md, "Goals"). Resources: the section's tools page, Google's Engineering Practices guide to code review, and SmartBear's "Best Kept Secrets of Peer Code Review" [BT] (docs/code-reviews/README.md, "Resources").

### Process guidance

"Code reviews should be part of the software engineering team process regardless of the development model." [V] Teams should learn to review in a timely manner, since PRs left hanging cause merge problems and go stale, losing work; qualified PRs reflect well-defined, concise tasks, so reviewing one should take relatively little time [AP] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/README.md, "General Guidance"). Guidelines [AP] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/README.md, "General Guidance"): establish a service-level agreement for code reviews in the team's working agreement; label tasks pending review or give them a place on the task board; check pending reviews in the daily standup and make sure they have reviewers; junior teams and teams new to the process can create separate review tasks; use tools; foster inclusive reviews.

If reviews take significant time to merge and become a blocker: measure the average time to merge a PR per sprint, review in the retrospective how it can be improved, assess it across sprints, and ping required approvers directly [AP] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/README.md, "Measuring Code Review Process"). On size, the page says that past a certain number of lines "the effectiveness of defects discovery will decrease" [V]; it is "not a matter of setting a code line limit, but rather using common sense" [V], and "More code there is to review, the higher chances there are letting a bug sneak through." [V] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/README.md, "Code Reviews Shouldn't Include too Many Lines of Code"). Automation (linting, code analysis, automated builds, tests and checks in CI) removes the need for "nits" and saves reviewers' time for design and functionality [AP] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/README.md, "Automate Whenever Reasonable").

### Author guidance

[AP] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/author-guidance.md, "Author Guidance"):

- **Describe the PR.** A descriptive title that sums up the PR in one short sentence; a description showing what changed and why.
- **Add relevant reviewers.** One or more, depending on project guidelines; ideally someone expert in the project or language. Adding someone less familiar helps check the change is understandable and spreads expertise. "In ISE code-with projects with a customer team, it is important to include reviewers from both organizations for knowledge transfer" [V] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/author-guidance.md, "Add Relevant Reviewers").
- **Be open to feedback.** Resolve a comment once the change is made; mark it "won't fix" with clear reasoning if not. For a change within the task's scope, "I'll do it later" is not acceptable; for one out of scope, create a new work item. Ask questions in the review rather than in private chat; if a thread bloats without conclusion, meet the reviewer (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/author-guidance.md, "Be Open to Receive Feedback").
- **Use checklists** of the PR's objectives in the description so reviewers can focus on key areas.
- **Link the task** to the PR; no need to duplicate information, but together they give context.
- **Annotate before review.** If a large PR cannot be avoided, explain the changes so the reviewer can see the goal of every code block.

### Reviewer guidance

"Since parts of reviews can be automated via linters and such, human reviewers can focus on architectural and functional correctness." [V] Their focus: the correctness of the business logic in the code; the correctness of new or changed tests; the readability and maintainability of the design decisions; and the team's checklist of common errors per language [AP] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/reviewer-guidance.md, "Reviewer Guidance").

- **Understand the code.** "Read every line changed." [V] With a stakeholder review, running the PR is not necessary unless it aids understanding. Read in a logical sequence rather than the tool's file order; open the whole file or check out the change for context; ask the author to clarify [AP] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/reviewer-guidance.md, "Understand the Code You are Reviewing").
- **Take your time and keep focus on scope.** Neither hasty nor overlong in one sitting; take breaks between demanding reviews. "Always remember that a goal of a code review is to verify that the goals of the corresponding task have been achieved." [V] Concerns about adjacent code out of scope become separate tasks (bugs, technical debt): "Don't block the current PR due to issues that are out of scope." [V] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/reviewer-guidance.md, "Take Your Time and Keep Focus on Scope").
- **Foster a positive culture.** Reviews should not be an arena for long discussions or "a battle of egos" [V]: "What matters is a bug caught, not who made it, not who found it, not who fixed it." [V] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/reviewer-guidance.md, "Foster a Positive Code Review Culture").
- **Be considerate.** Be positive and encouraging; prefix a point of polish with "Nit:"; use "we" or "this line" rather than "you", since reviews are not personal and language matters; prefer questions to statements, since the author may have a good reason; explain direct comments, preferably with an example; use the suggestion feature (GitHub, Azure DevOps) or a PR to the author's branch; if back-and-forth comments do not resolve a disagreement, talk directly or hold a group discussion, then update the PR with what was agreed and why [AP] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/reviewer-guidance.md, "Be Considerate").

The review then runs as two passes [AP] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/reviewer-guidance.md, "First Design Pass"; "Code Quality Pass"):

- *First design pass*: does the PR description make sense; do all changes fit this PR; are README or other docs updated, especially if the build changes; for user-facing changes, is there a GIF or photo, and do UI changes look good without unexpected behaviour; do the pieces interact sensibly; does the code incorporate the architecture and coding patterns.
- *Code quality pass*: **complexity** (functions too complex; single responsibility, "Function or class should do one ‘thing’."; should a function be split; "If a method has greater than 3 arguments, it is potentially overly complex." [V]; functionality not needed; easy to understand); **naming and readability**; **error handling** (graceful and explicit where necessary); **functionality** (race conditions in parallel code; unnecessary database calls; effects on the overall system; security flaws; variable names revealing customer information; correct treatment of PII and EUII, including logging); **style** (extraneous comments, since unclear code should be simplified, though comments may explain why code exists; adherence to the agreed style guide, with automated styling such as black and prettier); and **tests** (committed in the same PR as the code, with "I'll add tests next" not acceptable; sensible, with valid assumptions; edge cases handled; reading tests first can help understand the change).

### Pull requests

"Changes to any main codebase - main branch in Git repository, for example - must be done using pull requests (PR)." [V] PRs enable code inspection and automated qualification of code (linters, compilation, unit tests, integration tests), and their requirements "can and should be enforced by policies" [V] in modern version control and work-item systems (docs/code-reviews/pull-requests.md, "Pull Requests"). The general process [AP] (docs/code-reviews/pull-requests.md, "General Process"): implement against the task's well-defined description and acceptance criteria; before opening the PR, conform to coding conventions (partly via linters), ensure the code compiles and runs without errors or warnings, write or update tests so all new and existing tests pass, and update documentation; then submit the PR using the template and follow the review process to merge. A Mermaid sequence diagram shows a new branch, PR creation, review, code updates, merge to main and branch deletion.

**Size.** "We should always aim to keep pull requests small." [V] Small PRs are easier to review, easier to deploy (in line with releasing fast and often), and minimise conflicts and stale PRs. PRs should stay focused, around a functional feature, optimisation or readability, not loosely coupled code. "There is no right size" [V], but big PRs are harder and slower to review, and "We should always strive to have as small PRs as possible that still add value." [V] (docs/code-reviews/pull-requests.md, "Size Guidance").

**Best practices.** Every PR should be consistent, not break the build, and include related tests [AP]. Consistency means all changes aim at one goal, such as one user story; the page likens this to the single-responsibility principle at project level: "the PR should have only one *reason to change* the project" [V]. "Start small, it is easier to create a small PR from the start than to break up a bigger one." [V] Strategies for keeping PRs small: break into self-contained changes that still add value, release hidden features (feature flags, toggles, canary releases), or split by layer (for example with MVC or Observer/Subject patterns) [AP] (docs/code-reviews/pull-requests.md, "Best Practices").

**Description.** Well-written descriptions keep the change history clean; teams need not share a specification but should agree one at the start of the project.
