One popular choice is the Conventional Commits specification (`<type>[optional scope]: <description>`, with optional body and footer), with types often drawn from the Angular project's list; scope, body and footer are optional, while a required type and short description, in the page's words, "enables the features mentioned above" [BT] (docs/code-reviews/pull-requests.md, "Pull Request Description"). Resources include Google's approach to PR size, a "Feature Flags" article on martinfowler.com, and an article on Facebook's hidden-feature approach [BT] (docs/code-reviews/pull-requests.md, "Resources").

### Pull request template

The template, given as a fenced Markdown block, has sections for a work item link; a description of the change, its impact and the solution; steps to reproduce a bug and validate the fix (for bug work only), detailed enough for a team member to confirm the bug no longer occurs; a PR checklist (documentation updated; tests added to cover changes; all new and existing tests passed; code follows the project's style; lint checks produced no new errors or warnings; no other open PR for the same change); whether the change is breaking, with impact and migration path if so; testing instructions (OS used, test sets used, scenarios tried); relevant logs or outputs, with guidance on uploading long logs to Azure storage; and other information, known dependencies and follow-up TODOs [AP] (docs/code-reviews/pull-request-template.md, "Pull Request Template").

### Evidence and measures

Many code-quality assurance items can be automated or enforced by policy, and verification of main-branch policies in Azure DevOps or GitHub "may be sufficient evidence that a project team is conducting code reviews" [V] (docs/code-reviews/evidence-and-measures/README.md, "Evidence"). The evidence checklist [AP] (docs/code-reviews/evidence-and-measures/README.md, "Evidence"): main branches in all repositories have branch policies; all builds include appropriate linters and run unit tests; every bug work item links to the PR that introduced it once diagnosed, which "helps with learning"; each bug work item notes how it might or might not have been caught in review; the team regularly updates its review checklists with common issues; and Dev Leads review a sample of PRs or co-review to help everyone improve as reviewers.

Measures the team can collect [AP] (docs/code-reviews/evidence-and-measures/README.md, "Measures"): Defect Removal Efficiency (DRE), "a measure of the development team's ability to remove defects prior to release" [V]; time spent preparing for and in review sessions; and lines of code inspected per time unit or meeting. Tracking them manually, for example in a spreadsheet, is acceptable, as are platform dashboards and plugins. The page closes with: "since defects removed thanks to reviews is far less costly compared to finding them in production, the cost of doing code reviews is actually negative!" [V] (docs/code-reviews/evidence-and-measures/README.md, "Measures"). Its resource is Ganssle's "A Guide to Code Inspections" [BT] (docs/code-reviews/evidence-and-measures/README.md, "Resources").

### FAQ

- **Code review versus PR.** A PR notifies that a task is finished and ready to merge into the main branch; a code review is someone going over the code before merge, and can take place outside PRs. In the page's table, code review is source-code focused, intended for early feedback before a PR, and usually synchronous (meetings, over-the-shoulder review, pair programming); a PR has a broader scope (docs, integration tests, compiles), is not meant for early feedback, and is usually a tool-assisted asynchronous review that can be escalated to a meeting [AP] (docs/code-reviews/faq.md, "What Makes a Code Review Different from a PR?").
- **Why reviews.** Peer reviews are structured around best practices to find specific kinds of errors: "Much like you would still run a linter over mobbed code, you would still ask someone to make the last pass to make sure the code conforms to expected standards and avoids common pitfalls." [V] (docs/code-reviews/faq.md, "Why do we Need Code Reviews?").
- **PRs too large.** Size work items into small, clear chunks; commit early, when an individual item is done rather than the whole backlog item; make an incomplete feature switchable off until the full feature is delivered [AP] (docs/code-reviews/faq.md, "PRs are Too Large, How can we Fix This?").
- **Expediting reviews.** Slow reviews delay features and frustrate the team. Actions: a PR turnaround rule in the working agreement; a slot after standup to go through pending PRs; a dedicated PR review manager to keep things flowing; tools that show stale reviews [AP] (docs/code-reviews/faq.md, "How can we Expedite Code Reviews?").
- **Tools and enforcement.** The FAQ directs readers to the tools page for reviewing from Visual Studio or VS Code; branch policies enforce review rules [AP] (docs/code-reviews/faq.md, "Which Tools can I use to Review a Complex PR?"; "How can we Enforce the Code Review Policies?").
- **Pairing and mobbing.** For a pair, "Someone outside the pair should perform the code review." [V], since spreading knowledge of the code base to people who do not usually work in it is another major benefit of review; for a mob, a member who spent less or no time at the keyboard should review [AP] (docs/code-reviews/faq.md, "We Pair or Mob. How Should This Reflect in our Code Reviews?").

### Inclusion in code review

Reasons given for inclusive reviews: reviews are an important part of the job; "In ISE we work with cross cultural teams from across the globe." [V]; communication affects morale; inclusive reviews welcome new developers; and rude or personal attacks alienate, sometimes unknowingly [AP] (docs/code-reviews/inclusion-in-code-review.md, "Inclusion in Code Review"). Non-inclusive behaviours, with examples [AP] (docs/code-reviews/inclusion-in-code-review.md, "Types and Examples of Non-Inclusive Code Review Behavior"): inequitable review assignments (most reviews to a few people, others dismissed); negative interpersonal interactions (long arguments over subjective topics such as code style); and biased decision making (comments about the developer rather than the code; assuming one developer's code is always good and not reviewing it properly, or the reverse).

Inclusive practice [AP] (docs/code-reviews/inclusion-in-code-review.md, "Examples of Inclusive Code Reviews"): anyone and everyone on the team is assigned reviews; reviewers make clear whether a point is opinion, personal preference, best practice or fact; inclusive language and a suggestive rather than prescriptive tone; authors thank reviewers who improved the code or taught them something; and the "sandwich method" for a new developer or new customer, placing a suggestion between two compliments.

For authors [AP] (docs/code-reviews/inclusion-in-code-review.md, "Guidelines for the Author"): write code that is easy to read, review and maintain; make sure readers can understand the motivation and how the code achieves its goals; ask for targeted help; respond clearly to questions; and avoid huge commits, since large multi-file commits "will lead to unfair review of the code" [V]. The page's example: a huge commit from a senior developer may be approved without thorough review, while one from a junior developer may never be reviewed and approved [AE]. For reviewers [AP] (docs/code-reviews/inclusion-in-code-review.md, "Guidelines for the Reviewer"): assume positive intent; write clear and elaborate comments; separate subjectivity and coding choice from best practice, and discuss style and subjective choices in another forum rather than the PR; if you do not understand the code, do not comment that it is incomprehensible but call the author; and "Be suggestive and not prescriptive." [V], letting the author decide whether to accept proposed changes.

On culture, the page says ISE often observes non-inclusive review behaviour, that the culture and communication style of a geography influence how people interact over PRs, and that assuming positive intent is a good start to analysing review quality [AP] (docs/code-reviews/inclusion-in-code-review.md, "Culture and Code Reviews"). On the impostor phenomenon, defined via Wikipedia [BT], submitting code for review can be particularly stressful; everybody can make meaningful contributions. Tips for authors: follow the guidelines, and pair with an experienced colleague. Tips for reviewers: anyone can have valuable insights; fresh eyes are welcome; study the review until understood, check corner cases and look for improvements; ask simple, specific questions; compliment the author when you learn something; pair with someone to review where possible [AP] (docs/code-reviews/inclusion-in-code-review.md, "Dealing with the Impostor Phenomenon"). Tools named for inclusive review culture: Anonymous GitHub, Blind Code Reviews, Gitmask and inclusivelint [AP] (docs/code-reviews/inclusion-in-code-review.md, "Tools").

### Code review tools

The tools page links Azure DevOps guidance on customising task-board cards and columns, automatically including code reviewers, and configuring branch policies (in the UI and via the CLI, including an approval-count policy), and GitHub's protected branches. It gives step lists for reviewing in VS Code (GitHub Pull Requests and Azure DevOps Pull Requests extensions), Visual Studio (GitHub Extension for Visual Studio; Pull Requests for Visual Studio), and the web (Reviewable, for multi-round GitHub reviews) [AP] (docs/code-reviews/tools.md, "Customize ADO"; "Configuring Branch Policies"; "VSCode"; "Visual Studio"; "Web").

## Part VI: Team agreements: definition of done and definition of ready

### Definition of Done

Closing a user story, sprint or milestone requires verifying that the tasks are complete. "The development team should decide together what their Definition of Done is and document this in the project." [V] The page gives example checks [AP] (docs/agile-development/team-agreements/definition-of-done.md, "Definition of Done"):

- **Feature/user story**: acceptance criteria met; refactoring complete; code builds with no error; unit tests written and passing; existing unit tests pass; sufficient diagnostics and telemetry logged; code review complete; UX review complete (if applicable); documentation updated; the feature merged into the default integration branch (such as `main` or `trunk`) or per the agreed branching strategy; the feature signed off by the product owner (docs/agile-development/team-agreements/definition-of-done.md, "Feature/User Story").
- **Sprint goal**: the Definition of Done met for all stories in the sprint; product backlog updated; functional and integration tests pass; performance tests pass; end-to-end tests pass; all bugs fixed; the sprint signed off by developers, software architects, project manager, product owner and others (docs/agile-development/team-agreements/definition-of-done.md, "Sprint Goal").
- **Release/milestone**: code complete (sprint goals met); release marked ready for production deployment by the product owner (docs/agile-development/team-agreements/definition-of-done.md, "Release/Milestone").

### Definition of Ready

A user story picked from the top of the backlog needs enough detail to estimate the work to complete it within the sprint; if it does, it is Ready [AP]. "If a user story is not Ready in the beginning of the Sprint it increases the chance that the story will not be done at the end of this sprint." [V] (docs/agile-development/team-agreements/definition-of-ready.md, "Definition of Ready"). The Definition of Ready is "the agreement made by the scrum team around how complete a user story should be in order to be selected as candidate for estimation in the sprint planning" [V]; it can be codified as a checklist in GitHub issue templates or Azure DevOps work item templates, and works as a checklist that helps the Product Owner ensure a story has the details the team needs [AP] (docs/agile-development/team-agreements/definition-of-ready.md, "What it is"). Example items [AP] (docs/agile-development/team-agreements/definition-of-ready.md, "Examples of Ready Checklist Items"): a description with the details and input values needed; clear and complete acceptance criteria; the story addresses the business need; the acceptance criteria can be measured; the story is small enough to implement in a short time but large enough to give the customer value; and whether the story is blocked by unfinished work or another team's deliverable.

The checklist can be written by the Product Owner in agreement with the development team and the Process Lead [AP] (docs/agile-development/team-agreements/definition-of-ready.md, "Who Writes it"). Update it whenever the team sees missing information in stories that recurrently affects planning [AP] (docs/agile-development/team-agreements/definition-of-ready.md, "When Should a Definition of Ready be Updated"). "The ready checklist should contain items that apply broadly." [V] Items relevant to only one or two stories add overhead to writing stories [AP] (docs/agile-development/team-agreements/definition-of-ready.md, "What Should be Avoided"). When the highest-priority work is not ready, the page suggests: backlog refinement to check that high-priority stories have a clear description, acceptance criteria and demonstrable business value, and to break down stories too large for one sprint; prioritisation sessions to bring forward stories that unblock other high-priority work; and breaking blocked stories down to unblock part of their scope [AP] (docs/agile-development/team-agreements/definition-of-ready.md, "How to get Stories Ready").

## Part VII: Capturing non-functional requirements

### Goals and best practices

Non-functional requirements, "also known as quality attributes" [V], define a system's operational attributes rather than its specific behaviours: functional requirements say what a system should do, non-functional ones how it performs functions under specific conditions [AP] (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "Goals"). They generally increase cost because they need special implementation effort, but "by defining these requirements in detail early in the engagement, they can be properly evaluated when the cost of their impact on subsequent design decisions is comparatively low" [V] (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "Goals").

Best practices for documenting them [AP] (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "Documenting Non-Functional Requirements - Best Practices"): "Be specific: Avoid ambiguity and make sure the requirement is quantitative, measurable and testable." [V]; relate requirements to business objectives and the real impact of the system's behaviour; break them down to component or process scope rather than the whole solution; and understand trade-offs, since non-functional requirements may conflict and be hard to balance and prioritise.

### Template

A capture template, adjustable to the team [AP] (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "Template"): requirement name; description, including its importance and impact to the business; priority (High/Medium/Low, Must-have/Nice-to-have); measurement or metric; verification method (automated test, benchmark, simulation, prototyping); constraints (budget, time, resources, infrastructure); owner or responsible party; and dependencies (technical, data, regulatory).

### Taxonomy and example metrics

The page offers a taxonomy and "a framework for their identification, exploration, assignment of customer stakeholders, and eventual codification into formal engineering requirements as input to subsequent solution design" [V] (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "Examples"). Each attribute has a description and "Common Metrics", which are a mix of metric definitions and illustrative requirement statements with sample thresholds; they are examples, not reported measurements [AP] (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "Examples"). Each attribute name links to a per-attribute page outside this subset.

- **Operational** [AP] (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "Operational Requirements"): *availability* (uptime, with the downtime each threshold allows; see Key statistics); *data integrity* (error rate, accuracy rate and duplicate record rate, each defined as a percentage of total entries); *disaster recovery and business continuity* (backup and recovery plan, redundancy, failover and high availability, a disaster recovery plan, and regular testing and maintenance); *reliability* (example targets for MTBF, MTTR and N+1 redundancy).
- **Performance** [AP] (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "Performance Requirements"): *capacity* (maximum load, resource utilisation, concurrency, throughput); *performance* (example targets for response time, throughput, resource utilisation and error rate); *scalability* (example targets for load balancing, database scale, cloud request volume, microservice request rate and caching).
- **Security and compliance** [AP] (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "Security and Compliance Requirements"): *compliance* (pointing to Microsoft Purview Compliance Manager); *privacy* (compliance with GDPR, CCPA and HIPAA; anonymisation; encryption; respecting user privacy preferences); *security* (authentication, authorization, encryption, regulatory compliance; pointing to the Threat Modeling Tool); *sustainability* (energy per transaction; tons of CO2 emissions per year).
- **System maintainability** [AP] (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "System Maintainability Requirements"): *interoperability* (data format, protocol and API compatibility, with examples from health records and banking); *maintainability* (code complexity, code coverage, documentation quality, dependency management, code churn, with sample thresholds); *observability* ("The ability to measure a system's internal state and performance based on the outputs it generates, such as logs, metrics, and traces." [V]; system, application and custom metrics); *portability* (platform, hardware, file-system and data-format compatibility).
- **User experience** [AP] (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "User Experience Requirements"): *accessibility* (alternative text, colour contrast, focus indicators, captions and transcripts, language identification); *internationalization and localization* (language and locale support; multiple currencies); *usability* (task completion time, ease of navigation, user satisfaction, learnability).

## Key statistics (with provenance)

All figures below are the playbook's own statements. Apart from the IBM estimate, which the playbook borrows, they are recommendations, examples or illustrative thresholds, not measured results.

| Metric | Value | Classification |
|---|---|---|
| Unit test reliability | "should be 100% reliable so failures indicate a bug in the code" | [V] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Unit Testing") |
| Unit test speed | "should run in milliseconds, a whole unit testing suite shouldn't take longer than a couple seconds" | [V] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Unit Testing") |
| Cost of a production bug vs one caught in implementation | could cost 6 times as much (2008 IBM research study, as cited) | [BT] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/why-unit-tests.md, "Reduce Costs") |
| Reviewer complexity heuristic | "If a method has greater than 3 arguments, it is potentially overly complex." | [V] (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/reviewer-guidance.md, "Complexity") |
| Example reliability test case | 99.9% uptime over a month | [AE] (docs/automated-testing/test-planning.md, "Examples of Test Cases using the Given-When-Then Format") |
| Uptime thresholds and allowed downtime per year | 99% ≈ 3.65 days; 99.9% ≈ 8.76 hours; 99.99% ≈ 52.56 minutes; 99.999% ≈ 5.26 minutes | [AP] (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "Operational Requirements") |
| Example reliability targets | MTBF of at least 1000 hours; MTTR under 1 hour; N+1 redundancy | [AP] example (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "Operational Requirements") |
| Example performance targets | 500 ms response for button clicks; 100 concurrent users or 500 transactions per second; under 80% CPU and 1 GB memory; error rate under 1% | [AP] example (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "Performance Requirements") |
| Example scalability targets | at least 250 concurrent users across at least 3 servers; at least 1 million database records; at least 100,000 requests per hour; a microservices design handling at least 500 requests per second; cache of at least 10,000 records at a 95% hit rate | [AP] example (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "Performance Requirements") |
| Example maintainability thresholds | cyclomatic complexity under 10 or under 50 lines per function "is often desirable"; 80% or higher coverage "is commonly targeted"; documentation covering at least 80% of functionality; code churn under 20% "generally considered acceptable" | [V] / [AP] example (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "System Maintainability Requirements") |
| Example portability and localisation targets | at least three major platforms; at least five major languages | [AP] example (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "System Maintainability Requirements"; "User Experience Requirements") |
| Example usability targets | account settings completed in under 2 minutes; satisfaction of 70% or higher "typically considered satisfactory" | [V] / [AP] example (docs/design/design-patterns/non-functional-requirements-capture-guide.md, "User Experience Requirements") |
| Worked example: unit tests after the configuration fix is specified | 4 failing, 1 passing | [AE] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/authoring-example.md, "Fixing the Bug") |
| Worked example: mock over-specification | a test checking 5 web service calls breaks when the API needs 1 | [AE] (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Mocks") |

## Positions the author explicitly frames against

- *Heavy reliance on mocking frameworks and behavioural verification.* The mocking page argues that frameworks allowing call verification encourage tests tied to the implementation, recommends starting without a mocking framework and writing fakes where possible, and calls a seemingly essential framework feature usually a sign of insufficient abstraction (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/mocking.md, "Mocks"; "Conclusion"); the unit-testing page warns against adding a mock framework without weighing the risks of heavy mock use (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Mock Frameworks").
- *Writing too many E2E tests.* The CDC page frames CDC against the drawbacks of automated E2E tests and the tendency of teams to write too many of them, while keeping some E2E tests for the deployed whole (docs/automated-testing/cdc-testing/README.md, "Why Consumer-Driven Contract Testing").
- *Treating unit testing as sufficient.* "not the silver bullet"; abstracted dependencies stay uncovered, so integration or functional testing is still needed (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Conclusion"; "Abstraction").
- *Sleeps, disk reads and third-party API calls in unit tests* (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Things to Avoid").
- *Overusing dependency injection*: passing every interface into every class (docs/automated-testing/unit-testing/README.md, "Dependency Injection").
- *Too many or over-mocked integration tests, business logic in integration tests, and writing integration tests in production* (docs/automated-testing/integration-testing/README.md, "Things to Avoid").
- *Deferring tests or in-scope fixes.* "I'll add tests next" and, for in-scope review comments, "I'll do it later" are named as not acceptable (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/reviewer-guidance.md, "Tests"; docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/author-guidance.md, "Be Open to Receive Feedback").
- *Code review as a battle of egos, and non-inclusive review behaviour* (inequitable assignment, long subjective arguments, bias about the developer rather than the code) (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/reviewer-guidance.md, "Foster a Positive Code Review Culture"; docs/code-reviews/inclusion-in-code-review.md, "Types and Examples of Non-Inclusive Code Review Behavior").
- *Large, unfocused PRs and huge commits* (docs/code-reviews/pull-requests.md, "Size Guidance"; docs/code-reviews/inclusion-in-code-review.md, "Guidelines for the Author").
- *Blocking a PR on out-of-scope issues* (docs/code-reviews/process-guidance/reviewer-guidance.md, "Take Your Time and Keep Focus on Scope").
- *Narrow Definition of Ready items* that apply to only one or two stories (docs/agile-development/team-agreements/definition-of-ready.md, "What Should be Avoided").
